The awkward moment in capacity planning comes while the server still looks
healthy. All four GPUs are busy, aggregate token throughput is climbing, every
request eventually finishes, and the next user has already waited too long for
the first token. The machine has work left in it. The service has run out of
the kind of capacity it promised.

That happened at concurrency eight on four Intel Arc Pro B70s running
Qwen3.8-27B with MTP. The single-user row looked excellent: an 8K prompt
prefilled at roughly 4,000 tok/s and the stream decoded near 104 tok/s. At
concurrency eight the server emitted more output tokens per second than it did
at concurrency seven, but p95 time to first token crossed ten seconds.

So the capacity number for my reference agent turn is **seven simultaneous
8K-input, 1K-output sessions** under a strict p95 TTFT below ten seconds. Three
independent C=7 trials landed at 8.695, 8.697, and 8.702 seconds. Three C=8
trials landed at 10.656, 10.665, and 10.671 seconds.

The same machine can carry **22 simultaneous 2K-input, 512-output turns** on a
shared 12K serving profile. C=22 passed three times near 9.0 seconds. C=23 was
mixed, with one trial at 10.232 seconds, so I rejected it. This one profile can
serve both shapes. It doubles short-turn capacity over the native 256K profile
without changing the seven-session 8K/1K boundary.

The two boundaries separate the bottlenecks cleanly. The short workload was
limited by fixed recurrent state and decode graph coverage. The longer prompt
was limited by prefill compute before either resource filled. Changing the
same flags therefore doubled one boundary and left the other almost perfectly
still.

The trail from a Docker tag and an AIPerf C=1 row to those admission limits
includes the dead ends, the model architecture behind the
allocator warning, what each serving flag controls, and the raw-stream checks
that made sure the benchmark was counting generated text.

## Part I: Run the exact server

### Resolve `latest` into an experimental identity

The deployment tag on this machine is `latest`, which had been retagged to the
Qwen3.8 image. Tags can move, so the first benchmark command turns the tag into
an immutable digest:

```bash
docker pull rahulunair/sglang-xpu:latest
docker image inspect rahulunair/sglang-xpu:latest \
  --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'
```

The run resolved to:

```text
rahulunair/sglang-xpu@sha256:feb7b9130eff2fa26dfa09ab1a8b9a8423db013ad7d18f804f8b55a57cb2c175
```

I used
[`ulkaa/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4`](https://huggingface.co/ulkaa/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4)
at snapshot `2bf7f1646dc0875cff4404fdfef976cfb0ff2199`. The native-context
AWQ W4A16 checkpoint. Its BF16 multi-token-prediction head supplies the draft,
so MTP does not need a second model directory.

The public
[`rahulunair/sglang-xpu` recipe](https://hub.docker.com/r/rahulunair/sglang-xpu#qwen38-27b)
is the starting point. The command below pins the resolved image and launches
the final 12,288-token profile used for both workload boundaries in this post.

```bash
export IMAGE='rahulunair/sglang-xpu@sha256:feb7b9130eff2fa26dfa09ab1a8b9a8423db013ad7d18f804f8b55a57cb2c175'
: "${MODEL_DIR:?set MODEL_DIR to the pinned checkpoint snapshot}"
: "${CONTAINER:?choose a local container name}"

SERVER_ARGS=(
  python -m sglang.launch_server
  --model-path /model --served-model-name Qwen3.8-27B
  --device xpu --tp-size 4 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000
  --trust-remote-code --attention-backend intel_xpu --page-size 64
  --context-length 12288 --max-total-tokens 262144
  --chunked-prefill-size 4096 --mem-fraction-static 0.85
  --max-running-requests 64 --max-mamba-cache-size 128
  --disable-custom-all-reduce --watchdog-timeout 1800
  --cuda-graph-config '{"decode":{"backend":"full","bs":[1,2,4,8,12,16,20,24,25]},"prefill":{"backend":"disabled"}}'
  --skip-server-warmup --language-only --enable-cache-report
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder
  --strip-thinking-cache --enable-strict-thinking
  --speculative-algorithm EAGLE --speculative-num-steps 7
  --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 8
)
```

```bash
docker run -d --name "$CONTAINER" \
  --device=/dev/dri -v /dev/dri:/dev/dri \
  --group-add video --group-add "$(getent group render | cut -d: -f3)" \
  --ipc=host --shm-size=64g \
  --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE --security-opt seccomp=unconfined \
  --ulimit memlock=-1 --ulimit stack=67108864 \
  -p 30000:30000 \
  -e ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:gpu \
  -e XPU_REPO=/opt/xpu \
  -e XPU_DENSE_INT8_MAX_M=8 \
  -e XPU_SYMM_AR_MAX_BYTES=131072 \
  -v "$MODEL_DIR:/model:ro" \
  "$IMAGE" "${SERVER_ARGS[@]}"
```

The host ran a CachyOS 7.2.0 kernel and Intel driver 17012946. Each B70
reported 32,656 MiB. Tensor parallelism four places one shard on each card.
After allocation and graph capture, the 12K profile reported 10.59 GB of free
GPU memory, a 262,144-token shared pool, and a physical active limit of 25
requests.

### Readiness should not become a warm-up

I checked ordinary health, the advertised model, the launch arguments, and the
final allocator line before load:

```bash
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:30000/health
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/models | jq
docker logs "$CONTAINER" 2>&1 | rg -m1 'server_args=ServerArgs'
docker logs "$CONTAINER" 2>&1 | rg 'max_total_num_tokens' | tail -1
```

`/health_generate` sends a generation request. That request has a prompt,
graph shape, cache footprint, and compilation effect, so it belongs in the
workload if it is used. Plain `/health` tells me the process is ready without
quietly warming the path I am about to measure.

## Part II: Give capacity a workload and an SLO

### A fast single stream is only the starting point

The Docker Hub recipe begins at C=1 with 8,192 synthetic input tokens and
1,024 output tokens. I reproduced that row with AIPerf 0.10.0 before changing
concurrency:

```bash
aiperf profile \
  --model Qwen3.8-27B --url http://127.0.0.1:30000 \
  --endpoint-type chat --streaming \
  --tokenizer "$MODEL_DIR" --tokenizer-trust-remote-code \
  --isl 8192 --isl-stddev 0 --osl 1024 --osl-stddev 0 \
  --extra-inputs '{"temperature":0,"ignore_eos":true}' \
  --random-seed 42 --warmup-request-count 2 \
  --request-count 10 --concurrency 1 --export-level raw
```

| C=1 metric | published image row | this rerun |
|:---|---:|---:|
| TTFT p50 | 2.310 s | 2.133 s |
| TTFT-derived prefill | 3,546 tok/s | 3,840 tok/s |
| inter-token latency p50 | 9.03 ms | 9.619 ms |
| per-user decode | 110.7 tok/s | 104.0 tok/s |
| aggregate output throughput | 87.4 tok/s | 90.2 tok/s |

The rerun was close enough to show that the expected image, checkpoint,
attention backend, and MTP path were active. It still said nothing about the
queue that forms when several prompts arrive together.

A host-level capacity number needs the rest of its row. Input length decides
how much prefill work arrives. Output length decides how long existing decodes
remain resident. Cache state changes how much of a prompt must be recomputed.
The arrival process decides whether requests overlap at all.

### Fix the row before searching the boundary

My reference row represents a substantial agent turn: 8K input, 1K output,
closed-loop concurrency, and a p95 first-token limit below ten seconds.

| dimension | reference value |
|:---|:---|
| hardware | 4 x Intel Arc Pro B70, TP4 |
| model | Qwen3.8-27B AWQ W4A16 with MTP |
| configured input / output | 8,192 / 1,024 tokens, zero variance |
| server-visible prompt | 8,244 to 8,246 tokens after the chat template |
| sampling | temperature 0, `ignore_eos=true` |
| arrival | AIPerf closed-loop concurrency burst |
| cache | radix enabled, flushed before each independent trial |
| warm-up | eight C=1 requests, excluded from metrics |
| measured sample | at least `max(64, 4 × C)` requests per trial |
| latency contract | p95 TTFT strictly below 10,000 ms |
| boundary rule | all three trials at C must pass; test C+1 beside it |
| correctness | HTTP 200, exact output length, non-empty streamed text |

For workload row `w`, the measured limit is:

$$
C_{\max}(w) = \max \left\{C :
\operatorname{p95}(\mathrm{TTFT}) < 10\ \mathrm{s}
\text{ in every confirmation trial}\right\}.
$$

That definition gives admission control a precise job. Changing
the percentile creates a new result. The native maximum-passing rows in this
study all exceeded ten seconds at p99, so none is qualified for a p99 version
of the contract.

## Part III: Watch the tail break before throughput does

### The native 256K profile admits seven reference turns

I first measured the release profile at its native 262,144-token sequence
ceiling, 262,144-token shared pool, Mamba budget 48, and decode graph batches
`[1,2,4,8]`. Exponential probes and bisection located the reference boundary at
seven and eight.

| locator C | TTFT p50 | TTFT p95 | TTFT p99 | output tok/s |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 | 2.161 s | 4.101 s | 7.862 s | 178.5 |
| 6 | 2.126 s | 6.737 s | 11.409 s | 197.5 |
| 7 | 2.131 s | 8.694 s | 13.399 s | 218.5 |
| 8 | 2.135 s | 10.660 s | 15.583 s | 217.0 |

Median TTFT barely moved. The slow cohort carried the queue, and p95 rose by
more than six seconds between C=4 and C=8. C=6 would pass this p95 contract and
fail the same ten-second limit at p99. Picking the percentile after seeing the
table would be picking the answer after the experiment.

I then ran three fresh processes on each side of the adjacent boundary. Each
process received a cache flush, its own prompt corpus and seed, eight excluded
warm-ups, and 64 measured requests.

| C | TTFT p95, trial 1 | trial 2 | trial 3 | output tok/s range | verdict |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| **7** | **8.709 s** | **8.705 s** | **8.724 s** | 206.1 to 216.7 | pass |
| 8 | 10.674 s | 10.667 s | 10.669 s | 215.6 to 221.2 | fail |

The failing row produced at least as much aggregate output as the passing row.
The decoder remained productive while new prompts waited outside the SLO.

![](qwen38-capacity-planning/throughput-vs-slo.svg){fig-alt="Six native-profile 8K-input and 1K-output trials compare aggregate output throughput with p95 TTFT. Throughput overlaps at concurrency seven and eight, while every concurrency-seven trial stays below the 10-second SLO and every concurrency-eight trial crosses it."}

*Figure 1. Aggregate output throughput overlaps across the boundary; p95 TTFT separates every pass from every failure.*

Reading the points from left to right does not reveal a throughput cliff. The
vertical position carries the service failure. Peak tokens per second cannot
be divided into an ISL/OSL pair to produce a session count.

### Three request shapes produce three native boundaries

The 8K/1K row is the reference product shape. Two more rows show how quickly a
single host-level answer falls apart.

| AIPerf shape | server prompt range | maximum passing C | passing p95 TTFT, three trials | next C | adjacent p95 TTFT, three trials |
|:---|:---|---:|:---|---:|:---|
| 2,048 / 512 | 2,099 to 2,102 | **11** | 7.095, 8.751, 7.530 s | 12 | 11.402, 10.323, 12.015 s |
| 8,192 / 1,024 | 8,243 to 8,246 | **7** | 8.709, 8.705, 8.724 s | 8 | 10.674, 10.667, 10.669 s |
| 16,384 / 2,048 | 16,435 to 16,438 | **5** | 9.077, 8.617, 9.086 s | 6 | 12.656, 12.655, 12.660 s |

![](qwen38-capacity-planning/boundary-trials.svg){fig-alt="Three panels show independent native-profile p95 TTFT trials for 2K-input and 512-output, 8K-input and 1K-output, and 16K-input and 2K-output workloads. Every trial at the accepted concurrency is below ten seconds, and every adjacent trial is above it."}

*Figure 2. Each native workload has an adjacent passing and failing integer, repeated three times on both sides.*

The short row has the noisiest passing side, spanning 1.656 seconds across
seeds. The verdict still holds in all three runs. The reference row happens to
cluster within 19 ms, but that tidy repeatability is a property of these trials,
not permission to run one trial elsewhere.

![](qwen38-capacity-planning/capacity-envelope.svg){fig-alt="Maximum native-profile closed-loop concurrency under the same 10-second p95 TTFT SLO is eleven for 2K input and 512 output, seven for 8K input and 1K output, and five for 16K input and 2K output."}

*Figure 3. On the native 256K profile, the request shape moves maximum concurrency from eleven to seven to five.*

Longer input consumes the first-token budget directly. Longer output keeps
older requests in decode, so the next prompt arrives behind more resident
work. That second effect is easy to miss at C=1, where output length comes
after the only request has already received its first token.

The 2K/512 row exposed another puzzle. Its logical token footprint was nowhere
near the 262K pool, yet the native profile stopped at eleven client sessions.
The allocator had already printed the clue during startup: 64 requested
running slots had been reduced to nine.

## Part IV: Follow one request through Qwen3.8

### The model leaves two different kinds of memory behind

Qwen3.8-27B is a dense hybrid model with 64 decoder layers. Sixteen layers use
full attention. Forty-eight use Gated DeltaNet, a linear-attention recurrence.
The checkpoint also contains the auxiliary MTP head used here to propose up to
eight tokens before target verification.

One request therefore creates two different persistent objects inside the
decoder:

1. Full-attention layers append key and value pages as tokens enter the
   sequence. More cached tokens require more KV pages.
2. Gated DeltaNet layers carry a recurrent state forward. Its shape is fixed
   for an active sequence, so a 2K request and an 8K request each need one
   sequence's state even though their prompt compute differs greatly.

SGLang manages the second object through its Mamba cache machinery. The flag
is named `max-mamba-cache-size` even though Qwen3.8's recurrent layers are
Gated DeltaNet. Here "Mamba" names the runtime state pool, not a claim that the
model architecture consists of Mamba blocks.

![](qwen38-capacity-planning/model-state-map.svg){fig-alt="A schematic follows one sequence into Qwen3.8. Sixteen full-attention layers create KV pages that grow with tokens and draw from max-total-tokens. Forty-eight Gated DeltaNet layers keep fixed recurrent state per active sequence and draw from max-mamba-cache-size. Both paths use captured decode graph batches, which speed replay but do not count admission slots."}

*Figure 4. Attention memory grows with tokens; recurrent memory grows with active sequences. Decode graphs provide fast execution shapes for both paths.*

The two branches meet again during decode. MTP proposes a block, the target
scores it, accepted tokens extend the sequence, and both attention KV and
recurrent state advance. Graph replay can make those repeated shapes cheaper,
but it does not turn a long prefill into a short one.

### Five recurrent entries become one active request

In this pinned runtime, radix caching starts with three recurrent-state entries
per request. The extra-buffer policy used with overlap scheduling adds two.
The physical accounting is:

```text
recurrent entries per active request = 3 base + 2 overlap = 5
active request limit = floor(max_mamba_cache_size / 5)
```

That arithmetic reproduces every limit I observed:

| `max_mamba_cache_size` | physical calculation | runtime active limit |
|---:|:---|---:|
| 48 | floor(48 / 5) | 9 |
| 80 | floor(80 / 5) | 16 |
| 120 | floor(120 / 5) | 24 |
| 128 | floor(128 / 5) | 25 |

Client concurrency and active concurrency are different counters. AIPerf can
hold eleven sessions in flight while the runtime executes nine and briefly
queues two. That arrangement passes if the waiting cohort still receives its
first token before ten seconds. At C=12 on the native profile, enough requests
wait long enough to break p95.

## Part V: Separate the flags that look interchangeable

### Each limit controls a different axis

Several SGLang flags contain a large token or request number. Their names make
them easy to collapse into one idea called "cache size." They control different
objects.

| flag | object controlled | what the value means in this experiment |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `--context-length 12288` | logical maximum for one sequence | prompt, chat-template overhead, and generated tokens must fit below 12,288 |
| `--max-total-tokens 262144` | physical token-page pool shared by the server | attention KV for active tokens and retained radix pages draw from this pool |
| `--max-running-requests 64` | requested outer scheduler ceiling | the runtime may lower it when a physical pool supports fewer active requests |
| `--max-mamba-cache-size 128` | physical recurrent-state entry pool | five entries per active request resolve to 25 active requests here |
| decode `bs=[...]` | captured execution shapes | listed decode batches use graph replay; the list is neither a token pool nor an admission count |

`context-length` is an admission rule. It does not reserve 12,288 token slots
for every request. A 2K turn still uses roughly 2K prompt tokens plus its
generated tokens. Lowering this value helps only when the allocator can use
the released addressable range or memory for a resource that was binding.

`max-total-tokens` is the page budget across the server. Keeping it at 262,144
lets many short sequences share a large physical pool. It also leaves room for
radix-cached prefixes. Shrinking the pool may free memory, but it cannot reduce
the matrix work in a prompt that is already being processed.

`max-running-requests` asks the scheduler for an upper bound. The number printed
after allocation is the one the runtime can physically keep active. The native
launch asked for 64 and resolved to nine because Mamba 48 held only nine sets
of recurrent state.

`max-mamba-cache-size` sizes that recurrent-state pool. It scales with active
sequences rather than tokens in each sequence. Expanding this pool gave the
short workload room to move.

The graph list solves another problem. Capturing decode at batches 1, 2, 4,
and 8 gives those shapes a replay path without rebuilding the command stream
on every token. Extending the list through 25 keeps larger decode batches on
the same path. A missing graph tier can fall back to a slower execution path;
having a graph tier does not guarantee that its batch meets the latency SLO.
Prefill graphs remained disabled in every profile here.

Two nearby settings complete the picture. `--chunked-prefill-size 4096`
breaks a long prompt into 4K chunks so prefill can share the scheduler with
decode work. It changes scheduling granularity, not the total amount of prompt
compute. `--page-size 64` sets the attention KV paging granularity. Neither one
was varied in this study.

### Why the final sequence ceiling is 12K

An AIPerf `--isl 8192` message becomes 8,244 to 8,246 server prompt tokens
after the chat template. The server must then generate 1,024 tokens. A literal
8,192-token sequence ceiling cannot serve that request, even though it is
convenient to call the workload "8K/1K."

The final profile uses 12,288 tokens:

```text
8,246 maximum observed prompt
+1,024 requested completion
------
9,270 required sequence tokens

12,288 sequence ceiling
-9,270 measured requirement
------
3,018 tokens of headroom at the largest observed prompt
```

The 12K ceiling holds both benchmark shapes without reopening native 256K
admission. The shared physical token pool stays at 262,144. One number limits
the length of an individual sequence; the other sizes pages shared across the
host.

## Part VI: Change one resource at a time

### Lowering context alone leaves C=11 exactly where it was

I took the allocator's "KV cache capacity" warning literally and started with
context. Perhaps a 256K server paid for its maximum even when every prompt
contained only 2K tokens. I lowered only `context-length` to 8,192. The token
pool stayed at 262K, Mamba stayed at 48, and graph coverage still ended at
batch eight.

C=11 passed three times. C=12 failed three times. The context-only profile was
indistinguishable at the boundary because the nine-request recurrent-state
limit had not moved.

I then raised Mamba to 80 and extended graph capture through batch 16. C=16
passed at 7.197 to 7.220 seconds p95. Repeating C=16 with a smaller 65,536-token
pool produced 7.182, 7.190, and 8.231 seconds. The smaller token pool saved
space but did not buy capacity at this cell, so I restored 262K.

Mamba 120 with graph coverage through 24 passed C=20. Mamba 128 resolved to 25
active requests and graph coverage through 25. On the 8K diagnostic profile,
2K/512 passed C=23 three times and became mixed at C=24.

| profile step | context | token pool | Mamba | graph reach | measured result |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| native control | 262K | 262K | 48 | 8 | C=11 pass, C=12 fail |
| context only | 8K | 262K | 48 | 8 | C=11 pass, C=12 fail |
| state step | 8K | 262K | 80 | 16 | C=16 passes |
| smaller-pool A/B | 8K | 64K | 80 | 16 | C=16 passes, no gain |
| state step | 8K | 262K | 120 | 24 | C=20 passes |
| diagnostic edge | 8K | 262K | 128 | 25 | C=23 pass, C=24 mixed |
| shared deployment | 12K | 262K | 128 | 25 | C=22 pass, C=23 mixed |

![](qwen38-capacity-planning/profile-shaping.svg){fig-alt="For the same 2K-input and 512-output workload, lowering only the context ceiling leaves maximum concurrency at eleven. Larger recurrent-state pools with matching graph tiers produce passing steps at sixteen and twenty, a diagnostic 8K boundary of 23, and a shared 12K boundary of 22. Three shared-profile C=22 trials pass; C=23 has two passes and one failure."}

*Figure 5. Context alone changes nothing. Recurrent-state capacity and graph reach move the short row; the deployable 12K profile settles at C=22.*

The diagnostic 8K profile isolated the resource and reached C=23 for short
requests. It could not serve the reference workload because 8K input plus
template tokens and 1K output do not fit inside an 8K sequence.

The final 12K run keeps the larger recurrent pool and graph coverage, admits
the full reference request, and puts both workloads on one uninterrupted
server.

## Part VII: Build one profile for both workloads

### The shared 12K profile carries 22 short turns

The final server used the exact command from Part I. For 2K/512, each C=22
trial contained 88 measured requests. Each C=23 trial contained 92.

| C | TTFT p95, trial 1 | trial 2 | trial 3 | TTFT p50 range | output tok/s range | verdict |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| **22** | **8.988 s** | **8.998 s** | **8.988 s** | 0.690 to 0.918 s | 438.8 to 441.4 | pass |
| 23 | 10.232 s | 9.401 s | 9.400 s | 0.688 to 0.915 s | 421.4 to 447.6 | mixed, reject |

The C=23 median remained below one second in every trial. One slow cohort still
pushed p95 over the line. A median or a single lucky seed would have produced
the wrong admission setting.

The accepted capacity is C=22. Compared with the native profile's C=11, the
same hardware now admits twice as many short sessions under the same SLO.

### The same profile still carries seven 8K turns

I kept the server running and changed only the AIPerf workload to 8K/1K. Every
trial used 64 measured requests.

| C | TTFT p95, trial 1 | trial 2 | trial 3 | ITL p50 range | output tok/s range | verdict |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| **7** | **8.702 s** | **8.695 s** | **8.697 s** | 29.820 to 30.707 ms | 210.1 to 212.3 | pass |
| 8 | 10.656 s | 10.671 s | 10.665 s | 32.218 to 33.787 ms | 216.5 to 223.6 | fail |

On the final server, the two workload boundaries sit side by side:

![](qwen38-capacity-planning/shared-profile.svg){fig-alt="Grouped bars compare the native 256K and shared 12K profiles. For 2K input and 512 output, maximum concurrency rises from 11 to 22. For 8K input and 1K output, both profiles remain at seven."}

*Figure 6. The 12K profile doubles short-turn capacity and preserves the seven-session reference boundary.*

The extra experiment answers the context question directly. A smaller maximum
context can produce much higher concurrency when it is paired
with a larger recurrent-state pool and matching graph capture, and when the
workload was limited by those resources. The same profile cannot make every
request shape faster.

### The 8K prompt reaches compute before it reaches state

The native profile exposes nine active recurrent-state slots. The failing
reference cell is C=8, so all eight requests can already be active. Native
graph capture also reaches batch eight. Mamba 128 and graphs through 25 add
headroom that this cell never asks for.

The matched trials make that visible. Native C=7 measured 8.705 to 8.724
seconds at p95; shared-12K C=7 measured 8.695 to 8.702. Native C=8 measured
10.667 to 10.674; shared-12K C=8 measured 10.656 to 10.671.

![](qwen38-capacity-planning/matched-reference.svg){fig-alt="Four groups compare native 256K and shared 12K profiles for 8K input and 1K output. Both profiles pass all three concurrency-seven trials near 8.7 seconds p95 TTFT and fail all three concurrency-eight trials near 10.67 seconds."}

*Figure 7. Native 256K and shared 12K land on the same 8K/1K boundary, with nearly identical latency in every trial.*

The eighth 8K prefill crosses the ten-second budget. Increasing recurrent slots
cannot reduce those prompt matrices, and decode graph capture does not cover
prefill in this setup. The boundary comes from compute and scheduling before
state admission fills.

The short request reaches the fixed state ceiling first, so state tuning
doubles C. The long request spends
the TTFT budget on prefill first, so the same tuning leaves C at seven.

## Part VIII: Make every counted token prove itself

### Server token usage and streamed text must agree

An early C=8 probe reported one completion as 979 tokens when the client
retokenized reconstructed text. The stream ended with
`finish_reason="length"`, and the server's usage object reported 1,024 tokens.
Text reconstruction does not always invert the server's tokenizer exactly, so
the boundary runs use AIPerf's `--use-server-token-count`.

Server usage alone leaves another loophole. A broken endpoint could return
plausible counters with empty deltas. I parsed every raw SSE record and required:

1. The expected number of measured records is present.
2. Warm-up prompts are unique and absent from the measured set.
3. Every measured prompt is unique inside its trial.
4. Every response returns HTTP 200 and is not cancelled.
5. Every stream contains non-empty `reasoning_content` or `content` deltas.
6. Every final usage object reports the requested completion length.
7. Every request ends with `finish_reason="length"`.
8. Aggregate errors and output-length mismatches are zero.

The twelve retained shared-profile trials contain:

| generation check | total |
|:---|---:|
| measured HTTP 200 streams | 924 |
| exact server-counted completion tokens | 669,696 |
| non-empty generated-text chunks | 172,311 |
| generated UTF-8 bytes | 2,652,636 |
| errors, cancellations, length mismatches | 0 |
| streams finishing because they reached requested length | 924 |

I also decoded and read samples from the raw streams. They were continuous
model generations over the synthetic source text, not acknowledgements from
the load generator. Output hashes were unique within each trial.

Generation correctness is part of the capacity gate. A latency result is
discarded if the server shortens, cancels, errors, or fabricates the work that
made it appear fast.

## Part IX: Repeat the boundary search with AIPerf

### Use the automatic search as a locator

AIPerf 0.10.0 calls this a search recipe rather than a `tune` subcommand. The
monotonic `max-concurrency-under-sla` recipe is useful for finding the
neighborhood:

```bash
aiperf profile \
  --model Qwen3.8-27B --url http://127.0.0.1:30000 \
  --endpoint-type chat --streaming --use-server-token-count \
  --tokenizer "$MODEL_DIR" --tokenizer-trust-remote-code \
  --request-timeout-seconds 21600 \
  --isl 8192 --isl-stddev 0 --osl 1024 --osl-stddev 0 \
  --extra-inputs '{"temperature":0,"ignore_eos":true}' \
  --random-seed 42 --num-dataset-entries 72 \
  --warmup-request-count 8 --warmup-concurrency 1 \
  --request-count 64 --search-recipe max-concurrency-under-sla \
  --ttft-sla-ms 10000 --concurrency-min 1 --concurrency-max 64 \
  --search-style monotonic --num-profile-runs 1 \
  --export-level records --artifact-dir "$SEARCH_OUT" \
  --ui simple --max-workers 64
```

Search points can share more history than I want in a final claim, especially
when prompts wrap or the radix cache retains prefixes. I use the search to find
adjacent integers, then move each confirmation into a separate process.

### Confirm both sides from clean state

This template runs one boundary cell. Set `ISL`, `OSL`, `C`, `REQUESTS`,
`SEED`, and `OUT` for each independent trial:

```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30000/flush_cache
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:30000/health

aiperf profile \
  --model Qwen3.8-27B --url http://127.0.0.1:30000 \
  --endpoint-type chat --streaming --use-server-token-count \
  --tokenizer "$MODEL_DIR" --tokenizer-trust-remote-code \
  --request-timeout-seconds 21600 \
  --isl "$ISL" --isl-stddev 0 --osl "$OSL" --osl-stddev 0 \
  --extra-inputs '{"temperature":0,"ignore_eos":true}' \
  --random-seed "$SEED" \
  --num-dataset-entries "$((REQUESTS + 8))" \
  --warmup-request-count 8 --warmup-concurrency 1 \
  --request-count "$REQUESTS" --concurrency "$C" \
  --export-level raw --artifact-dir "$OUT" --ui None \
  --max-workers "$REQUESTS"
```

I use at least `max(64, 4 × C)` measured requests. With 64 requests, p95 is
sensitive to roughly the slowest four, which is the queued cohort the SLO is
supposed to expose. Three separate processes give prompt order, speculative
acceptance, and scheduler timing three chances to move that cohort.

Every Cmax trial must stay below the line. The next integer is measured beside
it. If C+1 is mixed, as it was for the shared short workload, C+1 is rejected
rather than averaged into a pass.

![](qwen38-capacity-planning/capacity-protocol.svg){fig-alt="A four-stage capacity protocol resolves the serving identity and workload, locates a concurrency neighborhood, confirms adjacent passing and failing points with three independent cold-cache trials, then validates raw generated text and server token usage."}

*Figure 8. Search locates the edge; independent adjacent trials and raw generation checks establish the capacity row.*

The machine-readable metrics behind the native workload surface are in
[capacity-data.json](qwen38-capacity-planning/capacity-data.json). The tuning
ladder is in
[short-profile-data.json](qwen38-capacity-planning/short-profile-data.json),
and the final shared-profile trials are in
[shared12k-short-data.json](qwen38-capacity-planning/shared12k-short-data.json)
and
[shared12k-reference-data.json](qwen38-capacity-planning/shared12k-reference-data.json).

## Part X: Turn the boundary into admission control

### The answer is a small capacity surface

For four B70s running this pinned Qwen3.8 MTP stack under p95 TTFT below ten
seconds, the measured homogeneous-workload capacities are:

| deployment profile | request ceiling | 2K/512 | 8K/1K | 16K/2K |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| native | 262,144 | C=11 | **C=7** | C=5 |
| shared | 12,288 | **C=22** | **C=7** | outside the profile |

If the service contract is the reference 8K/1K agent turn, the capacity answer
is seven simultaneous sessions. If the service handles 2K/512 turns and does
not need sequences above 12K, the shared profile carries 22. Those are complete
sentences an operator can turn into a semaphore.

The three native values describe alternative homogeneous queues. They are not
additive. A queue containing short and long requests creates a new interference
pattern. The next production experiment should replay paired input and output
lengths from real traffic, retain prefix-hit class and tool-use shape, then
search one total admission limit while checking p95 globally and per class.

Until that replay exists, the fixed rows remain regression anchors and
class-specific ceilings. A controller can keep short turns below 22 and
reference turns below seven, then become more precise when a measured mixture
replaces those isolated limits.

The operating limit may sit below the laboratory maximum. Rolling deploys,
traffic drift, telemetry, driver variance, and a week of requests are wider
than three benchmark trials. I would begin one step below the measured edge,
watch live p95 and queue depth, and raise it only after the production replay
shows the same margin. That policy buffer should remain visibly separate from
the measured Cmax.

The 4K prefill number from the first page never became false. It became one
coordinate in a larger answer. Seven 8K/1K sessions spend the ten-second budget
without filling the recurrent-state pool. Twenty-two 2K/512 sessions fill the
state-shaped serving envelope while staying under the same line. Capacity
planning starts when those two paths stop being called the same kind of speed.
